chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Dollar's Rise to Dominance

lessons.title: The Nixon Shock and the End of Gold Convertibility in 1971

body.text: On a Sunday evening in August 1971, President Nixon went on television for barely 18 minutes and quietly ended the monetary system Chapter 2 spent three lessons building. No currency on earth has been backed by gold since.

children.text: Chapter 2 closed with a warning: Bretton Woods had inherited Triffin's dilemma before that term even existed, the US had to run deficits to supply the world with dollars, but doing so for long enough would eventually undermine confidence in the dollar's gold backing. This chapter opens with exactly how that tension broke the system, on August 15, 1971, and how the US dollar went on to dominate global finance anyway, without any gold behind it at all.
The Slow Buildup: Too Many Dollars, Not Enough Gold

Through the 1950s and 1960s, the US ran persistent balance of payments deficits, partly the natural result of rebuilding a shattered postwar world with dollars, and partly the product of Vietnam War spending and Great Society domestic programmes that pushed up US inflation and government borrowing through the late 1960s. Dollars accumulated abroad in foreign central banks far faster than America's gold stock grew to back them. By 1971, foreign-held dollar claims exceeded the US gold stock by a wide margin, several times over by most estimates, a mismatch the fixed $35-an-ounce promise from Chapter 2 could not survive indefinitely.

body.text: France gave this abstract imbalance a very concrete face. In the mid-1960s, President Charles de Gaulle openly criticised what he called the dollar's exorbitant privilege, the same phrase this course used in Chapter 1, and began actively converting French dollar reserves into gold rather than simply holding Treasuries. According to widely repeated accounts from the period, France even used a naval vessel to help transport gold back from the US. Whether or not every detail of that story is precise, the underlying signal was unmistakable: America's closest allies no longer fully trusted the dollar-gold promise, and were quietly testing it.

markDefs.definition: The common name for President Nixon's August 15, 1971 announcement suspending the US dollar's convertibility into gold, effectively ending the Bretton Woods system designed in Chapter 2.
The informal term for the US Treasury's commitment, under Bretton Woods, to convert dollars held by foreign central banks into gold at $35 an ounce on demand; Nixon suspended this commitment in 1971.

children.text: In a television address that ran barely 18 minutes, President Richard Nixon announced what is now known as the
: the United States was suspending the convertibility of the dollar into gold,

that had defined the entire Bretton Woods system since 1944. The announcement was part of a broader package, a 90-day freeze on wages and prices to fight domestic inflation, and a 10% surcharge on imports to pressure trading partners into revaluing their own currencies. The gold window closure was framed as temporary. It was never reopened.

body.title: From Dollar Glut to Floating Rates, 1958 to 1973

events.title: The Dollar Glut Becomes Visible
events.description: Foreign dollar holdings had grown large enough that economists began openly questioning whether the US could keep honouring gold convertibility indefinitely.

events.title: The London Gold Pool
events.description: The US and major European central banks formed a pool to jointly manage the market gold price near $35 an ounce and ease pressure on US reserves.

events.title: De Gaulle Presses the Point
events.description: France began actively converting dollar reserves into gold and publicly criticised the dollar's exorbitant privilege.

events.title: The Nixon Shock
events.description: Nixon suspended dollar-gold convertibility, alongside a wage-price freeze and an import surcharge, effectively ending Bretton Woods as designed.

events.title: The Smithsonian Agreement
events.description: Major economies agreed to realign exchange rates and devalue the dollar modestly, raising the official gold price to $38 an ounce, an attempt to patch the system rather than replace it.

events.title: A Second Dollar Devaluation
events.description: The dollar was devalued again, and the official gold price raised to $42.22 an ounce, a figure still used in some US government accounting today even though gold trades far above it.

events.title: Major Currencies Float
events.description: The patched system failed to hold, and major currencies moved to freely floating exchange rates, the system still in place today.

children.text: From Fixed to Floating: A New Era of Fiat Money

markDefs.definition: Currency that has value because a government declares it legal tender and people trust it, rather than because it is backed by or convertible into a physical commodity like gold.

children.text: Since March 1973, the dollar and every other major currency have been

, worth what governments and markets trust it to be worth, not a fixed weight of gold. This is a genuine break from every system Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 covered. The classical gold standard tied money to a metal. Bretton Woods tied every currency to a dollar that was itself tied to gold. Since 1973, nothing physical backs any of it, exchange rates move daily based on trade flows, interest rate differences, and investor confidence, and central banks intervene when they choose to rather than by treaty obligation.

body.caption: Before and after the Nixon Shock

cells: Fixed at $35 (later $38, then $42.22) an ounce for foreign central banks
None; the dollar is not convertible into gold at any fixed rate
Fixed to the dollar within narrow bands, adjustable only with IMF approval
Freely floating for most major currencies, moving daily with markets
Ultimately, a promise of gold convertibility
Trust in the issuing government and central bank alone

children.text: India had kept the rupee pegged to the British pound sterling since independence in 1947, a direct continuation of the colonial-era arrangement from Chapter 2. Once sterling itself began floating after Bretton Woods collapsed, staying tied to a single currency that was now itself unmoored made far less sense. In September 1975, India delinked the rupee from sterling alone and pegged it instead to a basket of currencies of its major trading partners, giving India more control over its own effective exchange rate. This is a direct downstream consequence of the Nixon Shock, a decision made in Washington in 1971 reshaping how India managed its own currency four years later.

body.title: Advising a Central Bank in Early August 1971
body.scenario: You manage reserves for a mid-sized country's central bank in the first two weeks of August 1971. Rumours are circulating that the US may restrict gold convertibility, and you are holding a large share of your reserves in US dollars, much like most central banks at the time.
body.prompt: Based on what this lesson covered about the imbalance between the US gold stock and foreign dollar claims, would you have expected the Nixon Shock, and what would you have wanted to know before deciding whether to keep holding dollars afterward?
body.modelAnswer: A careful reserve manager watching the gap between the shrinking US gold stock and the growing pile of foreign dollar claims through the 1960s, plus visible signals like France's active gold conversions from 1965 onward, would have had real reason to expect some kind of break, even if the exact date was impossible to predict. After the announcement, the key question would not be whether gold convertibility was gone, that was now certain, but whether the dollar would still function as the practical reserve currency without it. The answer, which the rest of this chapter covers, turned out to be yes: convertibility ended, but network effects, deep US capital markets, and the sheer lack of a credible alternative kept the dollar dominant anyway. A reserve manager who sold all dollar holdings in panic in August 1971 would have missed exactly that shift.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: What did the Nixon Shock of August 15, 1971 actually do?
options: It raised the price of gold to $100 an ounce while keeping convertibility
It suspended the convertibility of the US dollar into gold, alongside a wage-price freeze and an import surcharge
It immediately moved all major currencies to freely floating exchange rates
It replaced the US dollar with a new international reserve currency called bancor
body.explanation: Nixon suspended dollar-gold convertibility for foreign central banks and paired it with a 90-day domestic wage-price freeze and a 10% import surcharge. Floating exchange rates only arrived later, in March 1973, after the Smithsonian Agreement's attempt to patch the fixed-rate system failed.

body.text: Figures on US gold reserves, foreign dollar claims, and historical anecdotes such as France's gold conversions in this lesson are presented as widely cited approximations for teaching purposes, and some details, like the exact circumstances of gold shipments to France, vary across historical accounts. This lesson is educational content on monetary history, not investment advice.

points: By 1971, foreign-held dollar claims far exceeded the shrinking US gold stock, the exact Triffin's dilemma imbalance Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 both warned about
On August 15, 1971, Nixon suspended dollar-gold convertibility, the Nixon Shock, alongside a wage-price freeze and an import surcharge, ending Bretton Woods as originally designed
The Smithsonian Agreement's December 1971 patch failed to hold, and major currencies moved to freely floating exchange rates in March 1973, a system still in place today
Since 1973, the dollar and other major currencies have been fiat money, backed by trust in the issuing government rather than any physical commodity

India's own 1975 shift from a pure sterling peg to a currency-basket peg was a direct downstream consequence of the Nixon Shock, and the next lesson covers how the dollar stayed dominant afterward through petrodollars
